name: cheating
description: The sensation of breaking a social rule that you view as justified in this case.
perceptions: I know there's a social rule for this context.
It's not critical in the large scale of things.
Everyone else does it.
I need to win or not lose.

guidance.description: If you find yourself cheating often, you might want to consider the roots of it. Is it loss aversion? Is it a sense that everyone cheats so you're dumb if you don't cheat? Does it make you feel clever? Are most rules seen as guidelines?
In the long term, cheating can harm an individual's reputation and career prospects. True success in the workplace comes from working hard, being honest, and playing by the rules.

variations.name: bending the rules
variations.description: The sensation of breaking a social rule that you view as a general convention that is meant to be broken when needed.
perceptions: I know there's a social rule for this context.
It's more of a guideline than a rule.
Everyone else does it.
It doesn't hurt anyone.

guidance.description: In order to bend the rules, it needs to benefit all, or at least not harm anyone. If it benefits you and harms the audience, the partner, or whomever, or if it gives you an unfair advantage over a partner, then bending the rules is not OK. With that said, we came up with the 'Top Four Reasons when it is OK to Bend the Rules.'
Choose to break the rules that limit you, not just because you don’t like them. Break the rules but consider the consequences on the rest, not just on you.

examples: skipping a step in the process

variations.name: someone else cheating
variations.description: Perception that someone's words or actions reflect selfishness when they were expected to do the 'right' thing.
perceptions: There's a social rule for this context.
Someone is not following the rule.
This person should have known and followed the rule.
results: Your reaction may range from laughter to anger to disgust. It depends on who's doing it, the importance of the rule, what they stand to gain, and how it affects you.

guidance.description: Encountering cheating in sports can be disheartening, challenging the spirit of fair play and integrity. When facing a cheating opponent, it's essential to handle the situation with poise and follow appropriate steps to address the issue. Here are practical steps to consider.

examples: someone calls the ball out when it was in

variations.name: relationship cheating
variations.description: Having an extra-marital affair of any type. There are many reasons people engage in affairs, but cheating creates outrage because it reflects poorly on one party and may create signficant costs.
perceptions: I'm not satisfied with my relationship.
It's ok to have a little fun on the side.

guidance.description: Cheating is a choice, and while certain elements can contribute to the likelihood of someone engaging in this behaviour, they don’t justify or excuse it. Here are 11 common factors that might lead to infidelity in a marriage. Understanding the context and reasons behind infidelity is crucial for effectively addressing the problem.

variations.name: someone ignorant of a minor rule
variations.description: Perception that someone's words or actions reflect selfishness in a minor way but they are not expected to know the 'right' thing.
perceptions: There's a social rule for this context.
Someone is not following the rule.
They might not have known the rule.
results: Depends on the rule, the person, the context

guidance.description: Here’s how to handle someone who is breaking a rule. (a) Handle it privately, (2) Ask if they realizes they were breaking a rule. (3) Give the person three choices: try harder, leave, or negotiate the rule.

examples: foreign traveller walking on the grass despite the sign
a very young child doing just about anything

variations.name: self cheating
variations.description: Breaking a rule you set for yourself that no one else knows or cares about.
perceptions: I made this rule for myself.
I'm not hurting anyone else by  breaking it.

guidance.description: It's your rule, so your choice. However, breaking your own rules too often could create negativity. Either don't make rules you know you won't keep, or consider the guidance for 'self discipline'.

variations.name: existential cheating
perceptions: I know there's a rule in my religion for this context.
I don't think this is a sin or it shouldn't be.
results: Anything from guilt to confession to excommunication.

guidance.description: Churchgoing people know how to follow rules. We also know how to skirt them. We know exactly where the line is, and how to stay technically in-bounds, even while we indulge in exactly what that commandment forbids. So here is a crash course on the Ten Commandments, focusing on the unique temptations we 'religious' people have against them.

variations.name: lying
variations.description: Speaking words that you know (or suspect) to be untrue but it's beneficial to you for others to hear them.
perceptions: What I'm saying is not necessarily true in a factual sense.
Everyone lies to get what they want. It's the way of the world.

guidance.description: Misinformation is everywhere. We're in a Post-Truth society now and verbal deception is apparently considered clever. However, if you're open to exploring the benefits of honesty and evidence, here are some articles.

variations.name: offensive deception
variations.description: Acting or appearing in a way that hides part of your true nature in a way that allows you to get an advantage over someone else.
perceptions: I'm hiding a portion of my true identity.
I want to gain an edge over them.

guidance.description: A deceptive appearance could be a gag, a sports tactic, or a prelude to crime.

variations.name: defensive deception
variations.description: Acting or appearing in a way that hides part of your true nature to protect yourself.
perceptions: I'm hiding a portion of my true identity.
I want to protect myself from others.
examples: driving a beater car when you could afford better

commentaries.quote: The more people rationalize cheating, the more it becomes a culture of dishonesty.
There's a reason behind every social rule. It's ok to formally renegotiate the nuance of a rule, but it's generally not cool to unilaterally consider yourself immune.
Lying is easy because 'truth' is difficult.

Spreading misinformation is the same as polluting the mental environment despite the opportunity for social praise. If you wouldn't toss a piece of garbage out of your car window, you shouldn't fib, stretch the truth, spin, or gossip. On the otherhand, if you like whales dying from eating too much plastic, you should consider going into politics.
I have no problem with cheating. Whatever you can get away with.
Cheating and lying can have long-term consequences. Trust is the foundation of successful working relationships, and when it is broken, it can be extremely difficult to rebuild.
